reviewed.suggested_tightening: Keep the slip-only/no-reporter-cite note, but make the short citation parenthetical match Va. Ct. App.

reasons: The opinion is a state appellate application of Fourth Amendment doctrine to a Flock ALPR camera system: "the City of Norfolk installed a system of 172 cameras at intersections on public roadways throughout Norfolk."
The court expressly analyzes Carpenter and distinguishes CSLI/dragnet surveillance from this Flock ALPR record, so the home role "Lower-court development (ALPR network)" is supported.
residual_risks: The role is a corpus taxonomy label, not a holding stated verbatim by the court.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Use "fixed Flock ALPR network" if the home page distinguishes fixed ALPR from mobile ALPR.

reasons: The facts match the holding: the cameras captured still images of cars and plates, stored license plate and vehicle-feature data for 30 days, and generally could not track a vehicle in real time.
The court states: "we therefore hold that the use of the Flock system in this case did not constitute a search that violated the Fourth Amendment."
The warrant point is supported by the conclusion: "the police were not required under the Fourth Amendment to obtain a search warrant in order to access the Flock system."

The Carpenter limitation is supported because the opinion says the cameras did not continuously monitor all travels, did not create an intimate window, and were not a detailed chronicle of a person's physical presence.
residual_risks: The opinion is strongly fact-bound; any reuse should preserve "on this record" and the current Norfolk configuration limits.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Keep the limits: current Norfolk system, public thoroughfares, still vehicle images, 30-day retention, and no real-time tracking.

residual_risks: Good-law and citator treatment remain for Lens B.
